title: Window frames and gaps-and-islands
goal: By the end you can say which rows a window function reads for each row (its frame), choose ROWS, RANGE or GROUPS on purpose, avoid the default frame's trap with tied rows and the LAST_VALUE surprise, and find runs of consecutive rows such as streaks of failed logins.

warmup.q: Account 900's first four ledger entries share created_at 2026-01-02 09:00, with amounts -100000, -80000, -30000 and -140000. What does `sum(amount_minor) OVER (ORDER BY created_at)` show on the first of them?
options: NULL, because the order of tied rows is undefined
One of -100000, -180000, -210000 or -350000, depending on the plan
warmup.why: With ORDER BY and no frame clause, the frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, and in RANGE mode the current row includes all its peers: every row with the same created_at. So each of the four tied rows adds up all four, -350000. The last option is what you get with ROWS and no tiebreaker.

sections.h: The default frame includes ties, so a running total jumps
sections.body:
Here is the start of a statement for account 900, the internal clearing account that funds every deposit, with lesson 6's running total, minus the tiebreaker:

```postgresql
 entry_id | amount_minor |       created_at       | balance
----------+--------------+------------------------+---------
        2 |      -100000 | 2026-01-02 09:00:00+00 | -350000
        4 |       -80000 | 2026-01-02 09:00:00+00 | -350000
        6 |       -30000 | 2026-01-02 09:00:00+00 | -350000
        8 |      -140000 | 2026-01-02 09:00:00+00 | -350000
       16 |       -50000 | 2026-01-10 09:00:00+00 | -405000
       18 |        -5000 | 2026-01-10 09:00:00+00 | -405000
```

The first line should say -100000. A batch job posted four deposits at the same instant, and all four lines show the balance after the whole batch. On 10 January it happens again. Nobody wrote a bug. The query says `sum(amount_minor) OVER (ORDER BY created_at)`, and this is what that means.

Lesson 6 said that with ORDER BY a row's window runs from the first row up to the current row. To be exact: every window function call has a **frame**, the rows of the current row's partition that the function actually reads. You can write the frame yourself, after the ORDER BY. If you don't, PostgreSQL uses a default, and with ORDER BY that default is `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`. In RANGE mode, CURRENT ROW does not mean this one row. It means the current row and all its **peers**, the rows with the same ORDER BY value (lesson 6's word). For entry 2, the frame runs from the start of the partition to the last row that ties with it: entries 2, 4, 6 and 8. All four get -350000.

One rule explains both shapes you saw in lesson 6. Without ORDER BY, every row of the partition is a peer of every other row, so the default frame is the whole partition, and you get a total. With an ORDER BY that has ties, you get a running total that moves in jumps, one jump per group of peers.

There are two fixes, and you usually want both. Make the ORDER BY unique, `ORDER BY created_at, entry_id`, so every row is its own peer group. Or change the frame's unit to rows: `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` counts physical rows, so the frame ends exactly at the current row. ROWS alone stops the jump but not the randomness: PostgreSQL still decides which of the four tied rows comes first, so the balances between them can shift from run to run. The tiebreaker fixes the order. Adding ROWS as well tells the next reader what you meant.

SELECT entry_id, amount_minor, created_at,
       sum(amount_minor) OVER (ORDER BY created_at) AS default_frame,
       sum(amount_minor) OVER (ORDER BY created_at
                               ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS rows_frame,

FROM ledger_entries
WHERE account_id = 900
ORDER BY created_at, entry_id
LIMIT 7;

refs.title: PostgreSQL 18: Window function calls (frames and peers)

sections.h: ROWS counts rows, RANGE measures values, GROUPS counts ties
sections.body:
Finance wants a 7-day volume line: for each March day with sales, that day's succeeded volume plus the six days before it. First fold the payments into one row per day with GROUP BY (lesson 4), then put a window over the day rows. The seed has sales on only seven March days: the 1st, 4th, 8th, 12th, 15th, 25th and 31st.

A frame clause has a unit, a start and an end:

```text
{ ROWS | RANGE | GROUPS } BETWEEN start AND end
start, end:  UNBOUNDED PRECEDING | n PRECEDING | CURRENT ROW | n FOLLOWING | UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
```

The first attempt counts rows: `ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` is the current row and the six rows before it. For 8 March it adds the 1st, 4th and 8th, 100810, but the 1st is seven days back, outside the week. On 31 March it adds all seven rows, the whole month: 211132. Six rows back is not six days back when most days have no row.

RANGE measures the frame in values of the ORDER BY column instead of in rows. `RANGE BETWEEN interval '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` takes every row whose day is at most six days before the current row's day. On 8 March that is the 4th and the 8th, 36810. On 31 March it is the 25th and the 31st, 53325. An offset in RANGE mode needs exactly one ORDER BY column of a type you can subtract from: a number, or a date or timestamp with an interval.

GROUPS counts peer groups. `GROUPS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, over payments ordered by day, takes the current row's day and the previous day that had payments, however many rows each holds. It is the rarest of the three. It fits questions like "this batch and the batch before it".

Two more tools. A calendar, one row per day (`SELECT date '2026-03-01' + n AS day FROM generate_series(0, 30) AS n`), with the volumes LEFT JOINed onto it, turns ROWS back into days, because then every day is a row; it also gives you the zero days, which you need for an average per calendar day. And a frame can leave rows out: `EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW` drops the current row, so `avg(amount_minor) OVER (PARTITION BY merchant_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW)` is the average of the merchant's other payments, the fair thing to compare a suspicious payment with.

Last, a trap from lesson 6's logical order. The seven days before 1 March reach into February. If the query's WHERE keeps only March payments, the window never sees February, because WHERE runs first. Read the extra six days in, compute the window, and filter to March one level up.

sections.h: LAST_VALUE reads the frame, and the frame ends at the current row
sections.body:
Risk wants every payment next to its merchant's largest and smallest succeeded payment, to see how far each one is from the extremes. `first_value(x)` and `last_value(x)` return x from the first and the last row of the frame. Sort each merchant's payments largest first, and first_value should be the largest and last_value the smallest:

```sql
SELECT merchant_id, payment_id, amount_minor,
       first_value(amount_minor) OVER w AS largest,
       last_value(amount_minor)  OVER w AS smallest
FROM payments
WHERE status = 'succeeded'
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY merchant_id ORDER BY amount_minor DESC);
```

first_value is right on every row. last_value is wrong on almost every row. At Volt Electronics it shows each payment's own amount: 129900 next to 129900, 75000 next to 75000. At Metro Transit it shows 550 for the 550 ride and 275 for the 275 rides, which looks right for the wrong reason.

The frame explains it. The window has an ORDER BY and no frame clause, so the frame is the default from the first section: from the start of the partition through the current row's last peer. The last row of that frame is the current row, or its last peer when there is a tie. That is why the three 275 rides show 275: they are peers, and the frame reaches the last of them. first_value works only because the default frame starts at the start of the partition. The PostgreSQL documentation warns that the default frame "is likely to give unhelpful results for last_value".

There are three fixes. Give last_value the whole partition with `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`. Or reverse the order and use first_value. Or, for a plain smallest value, use `min(amount_minor) OVER (PARTITION BY merchant_id)` with no ORDER BY at all. `nth_value(x, 2)` has the same trap: on the first row of a partition the frame holds one row, the second row is not in it yet, and you get NULL.

A named window can take a frame on top. `OVER (w ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING)` copies w's PARTITION BY and ORDER BY and adds the frame. The Try it uses that.

Not every window function reads the frame. Aggregates with OVER, and first_value, last_value and nth_value, do. row_number, rank, dense_rank, lag and lead ignore it: they work on the whole partition in window order. That is why lesson 6's ranks never jumped, and why `lag(x)` returns NULL on a partition's first row whatever frame you write.

sections.h: Gaps and islands: number the rows twice and subtract
sections.body:
Security locks a customer out after three failed logins in a row, and before they turn that on they want to see every run of consecutive failures, per customer, with its length. Here is Elena's history (customer 5): two successes, six failures in two minutes from 203.0.113.7, then her own success.

```text
success:  t  t  f  f  f  f  f  f  t
```

A run of equal values with no other value between them is an **island**, and the places where the value changes are the **gaps**. Elena has three islands: two successes, six failures, one success. "Runs of failures" is a gaps-and-islands problem, and it turns up everywhere: failed payments in a row on one card, days in a row with sales, how long an order stayed pending.

GROUP BY is the first thing to try, and it cannot work. `GROUP BY customer_id, success` puts Elena's three successes in one group, though they belong to two islands. Jonas (customer 10) is worse. He failed twice in April and twice in June, with a success after each pair. GROUP BY counts four failures and would lock him out, though he never failed three times in a row. GROUP BY sees which rows share a value. It cannot see whether they are next to each other.

The trick is to number the rows twice. Number all of a customer's logins in time order: 1, 2, 3 and so on. Then number them again, separately for successes and for failures. Inside an island both numbers go up by one per row, so their difference stays the same. Between two islands of the same outcome, the first counter keeps counting through the other outcome's rows while the second does not, so the next island gets a bigger difference.

Elena's failures have overall numbers 3 to 8 and failure numbers 1 to 6: the difference is 2 on all six. Her first two successes have difference 0, and her last success, overall number 9 and success number 3, has 6. The difference is an island id. Group by customer, outcome and island id, and each island folds into one row with a count, a first time and a last time.

Two details decide whether this works. Number all the logins, then filter to failures. If WHERE keeps only failures first, every failure is next to the previous failure in the numbered list, and Jonas's two pairs become one island of four. And an island id is unique only within one customer and one outcome: a success island and a failure island can get the same number, so group by the outcome as well, or keep only failures after the numbering.

sections.h: When the gap is measured in time, flag the starts and add them up
sections.body:
The two counters need "consecutive" to mean "the next row". Often it means something else. A login session is a burst of logins less than 10 minutes apart. A sales streak is a run of days with no day missing. Both are islands, but the gap is measured in time.

Build those in two steps. First flag each row that starts a new island, using lag (lesson 6) to look at the previous row: a login starts a session if more than 10 minutes passed since the customer's previous login, or if there is no previous login. Then number the islands with a running total of the flags (lesson 6 again). Every flag adds one, so all the rows up to the next flag carry the same number:

```sql
WITH flagged AS (
    SELECT customer_id, event_id, occurred_at,
           CASE WHEN occurred_at - lag(occurred_at) OVER w <= interval '10 minutes'
                THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS starts_session
    FROM login_events
    WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY occurred_at, event_id)
)
SELECT customer_id, event_id, occurred_at,
       sum(starts_session) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY occurred_at, event_id) AS session
FROM flagged;
```

A customer's first login has no previous login, so lag returns NULL, the comparison is NULL, and CASE falls through to ELSE: a new session, as it should be. Elena gets three sessions: 20 January, 19:40 on 6 March, and the burst that starts at 19:52. Her success at 19:58 comes 4 minutes 20 seconds after the last failure, so it joins the attack's session. With a 2-minute rule it starts a fourth.

The query needs two levels because a window function cannot take another window function's result as input in the same level: `sum(lag(x) OVER w) OVER v` fails with `window function calls cannot be nested`. The CTE computes the flags, and the outer query adds them up.

For whole days, the row-number trick from the last section works on dates directly. Take the distinct days with sales, number them in order, and subtract the number from the date: `day - row_number() OVER (ORDER BY day)::int`. On consecutive days the date and the number both go up by one, so the result stays the same date. A missing day makes it jump. On the large data set, merchant 1000 had sales on 160 of the 300 days, and its longest streak was six days, 6 to 11 May.

In Kotlin both methods are one loop with a counter: walk the sorted list, and start a new group whenever the value changes or the gap is too big. SQL needs the flags and the running sum because a query has no variable that survives from one row to the next. A window function is the way to carry information across rows.

analogy: Picture a stack of receipts sorted by time on a desk, and a card with a slot that you slide down the stack. For each receipt, the slot shows which receipts the function may add up: that is the frame. A ROWS slot is cut by counting receipts. A RANGE slot is cut by the time printed on them, so when four receipts carry the same minute the slot cannot split them and shows all four. A GROUPS slot counts piles of same-time receipts. Islands are runs of receipts of the same colour; numbering the whole stack and each colour separately, then subtracting, gives every run its own label. The analogy breaks at speed: you slide the card one receipt at a time, while PostgreSQL keeps a running state and, for sums and counts, takes off the receipt that leaves the slot instead of adding the whole slot again.
in_your_world: Payments systems post in batches, so ties are everywhere: a settlement file stamped 02:00, a payroll run, a Kafka consumer that writes a whole poll with one `now()`. Every running balance over that data needs a unique tiebreaker such as the ledger entry id, or the statement jumps. Fraud rules are frames: "amount spent on this card in the last 24 hours" is `RANGE BETWEEN interval '24 hours' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, not "the last 20 rows". Lockout and alerting rules are gaps-and-islands: failed logins in a row, card declines in a row, a Temporal workflow stuck in the same state for several checks. And sessionization of a click or event stream, with a new session after 30 minutes of silence, is the lag-plus-running-sum pattern from the last section.
mistake: Writing `sum(amount) OVER (ORDER BY created_at)` for a running balance over data that has timestamp ties, and testing it on data that has none. Hand-written fixtures have neat, distinct timestamps; production has batches posted in the same microsecond. The statement then repeats the same balance on several lines and the intermediate balances are wrong, while the final line is still correct, so reconciliation checks that only compare the last line pass. People make this mistake because the default frame is invisible and "running total" sounds like "one row at a time". Always end a window's ORDER BY with a unique column, and spell out `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` when you mean rows.

compare.note: Both find Elena's six failures. Oracle's MATCH_RECOGNIZE, from the SQL:2016 row pattern recognition feature, describes the streak as a regular expression over rows: PATTERN names a sequence of row types, DEFINE says what each type means, and MEASURES computes values over each match. It reads closer to the question and handles patterns that are awkward with window functions, such as "two failures, then a success from a new IP". PostgreSQL 18 has no MATCH_RECOGNIZE, so the same question is written with two row_numbers and a GROUP BY, or with lag flags and a running sum. Expect to rewrite MATCH_RECOGNIZE queries by hand when code moves from Oracle to PostgreSQL. Older Oracle schemas store flags as NUMBER(1) or CHAR(1), so their DEFINE reads `success = 0` or `success = 'N'`.

lab.title: A statement with ties, a 7-day line with gaps, and failure streaks
steps: With Docker running, run the tests from the `labs` folder. All six fail.

`seven_day_volume.sql` adds up the last seven rows. Make it add up the last seven days, including days in late February for the start of March.

Run the tests until all six pass. The second test of each exercise adds rows first: a batch inserted out of entry_id order, a February payment, a streak with no success after it, and another customer's login in the middle of a streak.
hints: `sum(amount_minor) OVER (ORDER BY created_at, entry_id)`: with a unique ORDER BY, no row has a peer. ROWS without entry_id stops the jump but not the random order of tied rows.
`RANGE BETWEEN interval '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` over the day column. Read payments from 23 February in the CTE, and filter to March in an outer query.

In a CTE over ALL logins, compute `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY occurred_at, event_id) - row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id, success ORDER BY occurred_at, event_id)`. Then `WHERE NOT success GROUP BY customer_id, island HAVING count(*) >= 3`.

drill.title: Islands for one customer, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write a query that lists every island of Jonas's logins (customer 10), successes and failures, with the outcome, the number of attempts and the first and last time, in time order. Then say what would go wrong if you put `AND NOT success` in the inner WHERE.

answer.src:
SELECT success, count(*) AS attempts, min(occurred_at) AS first_at, max(occurred_at) AS last_at
FROM (SELECT occurred_at, success,
             row_number() OVER (ORDER BY occurred_at, event_id)                        -- all logins
           - row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY success ORDER BY occurred_at, event_id) AS island   -- per outcome
      FROM login_events
      WHERE customer_id = 10) AS numbered
GROUP BY success, island          -- island ids repeat across outcomes, so group by both
ORDER BY first_at;
-- f | 2 | 2026-04-19 12:10:00 | 2026-04-19 12:11:00
-- t | 1 | 2026-04-19 12:12:00 | 2026-04-19 12:12:00
-- f | 2 | 2026-06-08 07:30:00 | 2026-06-08 07:30:40
-- t | 1 | 2026-06-08 07:31:30 | 2026-06-08 07:31:30
-- With NOT success in the inner WHERE, the successes are gone before the numbering, both
-- counters move together on every failure, and all four failures become one island.

recap: A frame is the set of rows of the current row's partition that a window function reads. With ORDER BY and no frame clause it is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW.
In RANGE mode, CURRENT ROW includes every peer, so tied rows share one running total. End the ORDER BY with a unique column, and write ROWS when you mean rows.
ROWS counts rows, RANGE measures the ORDER BY value (`interval '6 days' PRECEDING`), GROUPS counts peer groups. When days are missing, rows are not days.
last_value and nth_value read the frame, so give them `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`, or use first_value or min and max instead.
Islands: row_number over all rows minus row_number within the value is constant inside a run. For gaps in time, flag the starts with lag and add the flags up.

quiz.q: `count(*) OVER (ORDER BY day)` over payments shows 3, 3, 3 on the three payments of one day. Which change makes it count 1, 2, 3 within that day, in the same order every time?
options: Add `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`
Add `payment_id` to the window's ORDER BY
Add `PARTITION BY day`
Write `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` explicitly
quiz.why: With a unique ORDER BY no row has a peer, so the default frame ends exactly at the current row, and the order of the three payments is fixed by their ids. ROWS alone also counts 1, 2, 3, but which payment gets which number is up to PostgreSQL. PARTITION BY day restarts the count each day but keeps the tie inside it. Writing the default frame explicitly changes nothing.

quiz.q: Daily volumes exist for 1, 2, 3, 7 and 8 June. On which days do `ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` and `RANGE BETWEEN interval '2 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` give different sums?
options: Only on 3 June
Only on 1 June
On none of them
On 7 and 8 June
quiz.why: Up to 3 June the rows are consecutive days, so two rows back is two days back. On 7 June, ROWS takes the 2nd, 3rd and 7th, while RANGE takes 5 to 7 June, which holds only the 7th. On 8 June, ROWS takes the 3rd, 7th and 8th, and RANGE only the 7th and 8th. ROWS counts rows whatever days they are.

quiz.q: `last_value(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY card_id ORDER BY created_at)` is meant to show each card's latest payment time on every row. What does it show?
options: Each row's own created_at, or its last tied peer's
The card's latest payment time, on every row
NULL except on the card's last row
The card's first payment time
quiz.why: The default frame ends at the current row's last peer, so the last row of the frame is the current row (or a row tied with it). Add `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`, or use `max(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY card_id)`.

quiz.q: You compute the island id as `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY occurred_at) - row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id, success ORDER BY occurred_at)` but add `WHERE NOT success` to that same query. What happens to Jonas, who failed twice, succeeded, and failed twice again?
options: Each failure becomes its own island
PostgreSQL rejects a WHERE next to window functions
His four failures become one island, because the success between them was removed before the numbering
It still finds his two islands of two
quiz.why: WHERE runs before window functions. With the success gone, both counters count the same four rows, the difference is 0 on all of them, and the runs merge. Number every login first, then keep the failures one level up.

quiz.q: Lesson 6 filtered on a window's result one query level up. You want only the March days whose 7-day volume is above 100,000 cents. Where does that condition go?
options: In WHERE: `WHERE sum(volume_minor) OVER (ORDER BY day RANGE BETWEEN interval '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) > 100000`
In HAVING, next to the GROUP BY that folds the payments into days
In the outer query: compute the 7-day sum in a subquery or CTE, then `WHERE volume_7d_minor > 100000` around it
In the frame: `RANGE BETWEEN 100000 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`
quiz.why: Window functions run after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, so neither WHERE nor HAVING can see the 7-day sum: PostgreSQL rejects both with `window functions are not allowed in WHERE` (or `in HAVING`). Name the sum one level down and filter outside it. The frame says which rows each sum reads, not which rows the query returns. PostgreSQL 18 has no QUALIFY clause to save the extra level.

flashcards.back: The rows of the current row's partition that a window function actually reads. The ORDER BY and the frame clause decide it.

flashcards.front: What is the default frame when OVER has an ORDER BY?
flashcards.back: RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW: from the partition's start through the current row's last peer.

flashcards.front: Why does a running sum repeat a value on tied rows?
flashcards.back: In RANGE mode CURRENT ROW includes all peers, so tied rows share one frame. Add a unique tiebreaker, and ROWS.

flashcards.front: ROWS, RANGE or GROUPS: which one measures values?
flashcards.back: RANGE. ROWS counts rows, GROUPS counts peer groups, RANGE takes rows whose ORDER BY value is within an offset such as `interval '6 days'`.

flashcards.front: How do you make last_value return the partition's last value?
flashcards.back: Give it the whole partition: `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`. Or use first_value with the opposite order.

flashcards.front: What is the two-counter trick for islands?
flashcards.back: row_number over all rows minus row_number within each value. It stays constant inside a run, so it names the island.

flashcards.front: How do you split islands by a time gap?
flashcards.back: Flag a row when lag shows a gap over the limit (or no previous row), then a running sum of the flags numbers the islands.

terms.plain: The subset of the partition that a window function reads for the current row.
A frame measured in physical rows: `6 PRECEDING` means six rows back.
A frame measured in the ORDER BY value: `interval '6 days' PRECEDING` means six days back. CURRENT ROW includes all peers.
A frame measured in peer groups: `1 PRECEDING` means the previous set of tied rows.
All rows that tie on the window's ORDER BY.
An island is a run of consecutive rows with the same value; a gap is where the value changes or time jumps.
A frame option that leaves out the current row, its peers, or the other ties.

explain_back.prompt: A dashboard shows a running total of daily deposits that sometimes jumps by two deposits at once, and a "balance at end of month" column written with last_value that just repeats each row's own balance. Explain both bugs with the word frame, and fix them.
explain_back.answer: Both come from the default frame. With ORDER BY and no frame clause, a window function reads RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, and in RANGE mode the current row includes all its peers, the rows with the same ORDER BY value. Two deposits with the same timestamp are peers, so each one's running total already includes the other: the total jumps by both at once. The fix is a unique ORDER BY, such as created_at then the deposit id, plus ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW to say it plainly. last_value returns the last row of the frame, and the default frame ends at the current row, so it returns the current row's own balance. To get the month's last balance, give it the whole partition, PARTITION BY month with ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING, or take first_value with the order reversed.

deeper.body:
The frame clause has one more part. After the end you can write `EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW` (drop the current row), `EXCLUDE GROUP` (drop the current row and its peers), `EXCLUDE TIES` (drop the peers but keep the current row) or `EXCLUDE NO OTHERS`, the default. `EXCLUDE GROUP` is how you compare a payment with the other days, not with payments made at the same instant.

Frames are cheap for some functions and not others. For `sum`, `count` and `avg`, PostgreSQL can keep a running state and, when a row leaves a moving frame such as `6 PRECEDING`, subtract it instead of adding the whole frame again; the documentation calls this moving-aggregate mode, and it needs an inverse function for the aggregate. `min` and `max` have no inverse, so a sliding maximum over a large frame re-scans the frame each time the old maximum leaves it. On frames of a few rows the difference does not matter; on a 10,000-row sliding frame it does.

RANGE has a cost of its own. To know where the current row's peer group ends, PostgreSQL has to look ahead past the current row. ROWS does not, which is why EXPLAIN often shows `ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING` for functions that do not depend on the frame: the planner switches to the cheaper mode when the result cannot change.

The two-counter trick generalises. Any value that defines "the same run" can go in the second PARTITION BY: the status of an order, the IP address of a login, the merchant of a payment. And a run can be defined by more than one rule at once, for example "failures from the same IP with less than a minute between them", by combining a lag-based flag for the time gap with a flag for a change of IP, and adding up either.

Oracle and the SQL:2016 standard have row pattern recognition, MATCH_RECOGNIZE, for when the pattern is more than a run of one value. PostgreSQL 18 does not have it, so the techniques in this lesson are what you use instead.
